# Markets, [measured.]{.grad}

Each question gets a naive baseline to beat, a stated uncertainty, and an honest
answer, including when the answer is "it didn't work".

[The method]{.eyebrow}

## Four rules, every time {.section-title}

:::: {.steps}

::: {.step}
`<i class="bi bi-flag"></i>`{=html}

#### Baselines first

A model only counts if it beats the simplest possible answer, such as "it always
goes up".
:::

::: {.step}
`<i class="bi bi-eye-slash"></i>`{=html}

#### No peeking

Every call is made by a model that has only seen the days before it. Tests fail if
the future leaks in.
:::

::: {.step}
`<i class="bi bi-arrows-collapse-vertical"></i>`{=html}

#### Uncertainty shown

Every number comes with the range it plausibly lies in. If a difference could be
zero, it is reported as no difference.
:::

::: {.step}
`<i class="bi bi-journal-check"></i>`{=html}

#### Live log decides

Predictions are written down before the market opens and scored afterwards, in a
record that cannot be edited.
:::

[Experiment · live]{.tag .live}

### NVIDIA predictor

Can machine learning beat naive baselines at predicting whether NVDA closes up or
down the next day? Models are tested on two decades of history and then scored
daily on predictions they cannot take back.

[Open the experiment →](experiments/nvidia.qmd){.card-link}
:::
